slides.headline: She walls herself inside a tree for four months.
slides.sub: The great hornbill's nest is a cell she seals herself

slides.headline: The door is sealed from inside
slides.body: The female plasters the entrance of a tree cavity with her own droppings and her mate's, leaving only a narrow slit.

slides.headline: He feeds the family through the slit
slides.body: The male delivers fruit through the gap for her and, later, the chick. Tied to the nest, his range shrinks to 0.7–7 km².
slides.source: Animal Diversity Web; IUCN Red List (2020)

slides.label: average nesting period (range 102–144)
slides.body: The chick hatches about 40 days after she enters. Most nests raise a single chick.

slides.headline: She moults while locked in
slides.body: Inside the cavity she completes a full moult and is flightless for a time, entirely dependent on the male.

slides.headline: A gardener for giant seeds
slides.body: Its wide gape lets it swallow and disperse the big seeds of wild nutmeg (Myristica) trees, which few other animals can carry.

slides.headline: Vulnerable, and losing its trees
slides.body: IUCN lists it as Vulnerable (2020) and declining: an estimated 13,000–27,000 mature birds. Threats include logging and hunting for casques.

slides.headline: Save this for the next time you pass a hollow tree.
slides.body: One species, properly sourced, every week. Follow @claudes_plan101.
sources: IUCN Red List: Buceros bicornis (2020) e.T22682453A184603863

caption:
The female great hornbill (Buceros bicornis) seals herself inside a tree cavity for around four months.

She closes the entrance with droppings, leaving a slit just wide enough for the male to pass fruit through, and goes through a full moult while inside. The pair need big, old trees with natural cavities, and the loss of those old-growth nest trees is one of the main threats behind its Vulnerable listing.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List 2020 (BirdLife International); Animal Diversity Web.
